mcqs.question: Which React Testing Library query is the best fit when an alert should not be present immediately after rendering?
options: `getByRole('alert')`
`queryByRole('alert')`
`findByRole('alert')`
`getAllByRole('alert')`
mcqs.explanation: `queryBy` returns null for zero matches, which suits a negative assertion. `findBy` is for an element expected to appear asynchronously, not for every absence check.

mcqs.question: A test file holds `const now = jest.spyOn(Date, 'now').mockReturnValue(0)` at module scope and calls `now.mockClear()` in `afterEach`. A later test in the same file asserts the real wall clock and receives `0`. Which change fixes the leak, and why?
options: Call `now.mockReset()` instead: it removes the fake from the spy and returns `Date.now` to its normal implementation.
Call `now.mockRestore()` instead: `mockClear` erases calls but keeps the fake, and only restoring puts the original back — valid here because `jest.spyOn` created it.
Keep `mockClear` and add `jest.clearAllMocks()`, whose global sweep also drops implementations left behind by earlier files.
Move the `jest.spyOn` call into the one test that needs it: a mock created inside a test is discarded when that test ends.
mcqs.explanation: The leak is behavior, not history: the spy still resolves to `0` in every later test, and `mockClear()` never touches implementations — it only empties `mock.calls`, `mock.results`, `mock.instances` and `mock.contexts` (https://jestjs.io/docs/mock-function-api). `mockRestore()` does what `mockReset()` does and then restores the original implementation, which is the only one of the three that undoes a `spyOn`. The strongest distractor is option 0: `mockReset` sounds like 'back to normal', but it replaces the implementation with an empty function returning `undefined`, so the later test would receive `undefined` instead of `0` — a different failure, not a fix. Option 2 repeats the same mistake at a wider scope, because `jest.clearAllMocks()` is `mockClear` for every mock, and option 3 is the scope illusion: Jest isolates modules per file, not per test, so a spy created inside a test keeps applying to whatever runs after it unless it is restored.

mcqs.question: A status label is mounted on the first render and its text changes from `Saving…` to `Saved` when the request settles. Which assertion fails only when the text is wrong, instead of depending on when the DOM happens to be read?
options: `expect(await page.getByRole('status').textContent()).toBe('Saved')` — awaiting the read waits for the settled value.
`await page.getByRole('status').waitFor({ state: 'attached' }); expect(await page.getByRole('status').textContent()).toBe('Saved')` — the explicit wait makes the read safe.
`await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toHaveText('Saved')` — the web-first assertion re-fetches the locator and re-checks until the text matches or the timeout expires.
`await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toBeAttached()` — it is a retrying assertion, so it waits for the update as well.
mcqs.explanation: `toHaveText` belongs to the auto-retrying family: it re-fetches the element and re-checks the condition until it passes or the assertion timeout expires (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-assertions), which is exactly the 'text changes later' case. `textContent()` is a read that returns the current value — awaiting it synchronizes with the round trip, not with the UI transition — and a generic `expect` around a string cannot retry. The strongest distractor is option 1: `waitFor()` is the deliberate-sounding explicit wait, but it resolves on a state this label satisfies from the first render, so it returns immediately and the race is untouched. Option 3 fails from the other direction: it retries, but it retries the wrong contract, going green while the label still reads `Saving…`. Both are waits for something already true, which is why they look safe in review.

mcqs.question: A toolbar refactor wraps the primary button in two new `div`s and 30 Playwright tests fail with 'locator resolved to 0 elements'. Their locator was `page.locator('.modal-footer > button.primary')`. Which replacement ties the test to behavior instead of to today's markup?
options: `page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save order' })` — role plus accessible name is the contract the control publishes to assistive technology.
`page.locator('button.primary')` — dropping the parent chain removes the dependency on the toolbar's structure.
`page.locator('button').nth(2)` — a positional locator survives markup changes as long as the order of controls is stable.
`page.getByTestId('save-order')` on every toolbar element — test ids never break, so the suite stops failing on redesigns.
mcqs.explanation: A role with an accessible name is the user-facing contract: it is what a screen reader announces and what Playwright documents as the first choice, so an added wrapper is invisible to the test while a dropped label fails it (https://playwright.dev/docs/best-practices). The strongest distractor is option 3, because 'use a test id everywhere' sounds like the mature lesson from a flaky suite: it does remove the breakage, and it removes the coverage with it — a test id keeps matching after the accessible name disappears, which is precisely the regression this product should not ship. Option 1 still describes markup (a class can be renamed, or shared by three buttons, and `.primary` is a styling detail), and option 2 trades structure for order, so inserting one control breaks it again. Test ids stay legitimate for the residue with no user-facing contract — a canvas or a third-party widget — not as the default.

mcqs.question: A component test replaced `jest.spyOn(ordersClient, 'create')` with an MSW handler for `POST /api/orders` that answers `{ data: { id: '42', status: 'paid' } }`. Which statement describes what the test proves now?
options: It proves the production endpoint accepts this payload, so the contract test on the order shape can be dropped.
It lets the test skip the visible assertion: once the handler controls the response, asserting the rendered result only re-checks the mock.
It keeps the client's request building, the envelope unwrapping and the component's state transitions real, so a defect in any of them fails the test.
It removes the need to reset state between tests, because request handlers hold no state that can leak into a later test.
mcqs.explanation: A boundary mock replaces the server, not the application: the real client still builds the request (URL, method, headers, serialization), still parses the envelope, and the component still walks loading → success or error, which is where integration defects live (https://mswjs.io/docs/). The strongest distractor is option 0: a handler is indeed closer to production than a function spy, but the handler is authored by the same team, so nothing verifies that the real producer accepts the payload — that remains a contract or end-to-end concern. Option 3 inverts MSW's lifecycle, since handlers registered with `server.use` persist for the rest of the file unless `resetHandlers()` runs, which is why the setup resets them after each test. Option 1 is the tautology trap: the handler fixes the response, and the assertion is what proves the component turned that response into the right screen; remove it and the test passes when nothing renders.

mcqs.question: A dialog ships with an axe scan that stays green in CI. Support then reports that Escape does not close it and that focus stays trapped behind it. Which explanation fits the evidence?
options: The scan applies a fixed rule set to the rendered DOM: keyboard operability and focus management are behavior, so a separate keyboard spec has to cover them.
The scan missed the dialog because it renders in a portal outside the scanned root, so including that subtree would have caught both defects.
A clean scan proves WCAG conformance, so the remaining defects are browser or screen-reader bugs rather than accessibility defects.
The scan should be replaced by manual testing, because automated rules cannot find enough to justify running them on every commit.
mcqs.explanation: Automated scans apply a rule set to the rendered DOM; they catch a minority of success criteria — missing names, invalid roles, duplicate ids, some contrast failures — and cannot observe what a person does with the keyboard (https://www.w3.org/WAI/test-evaluate/). Escape handling and focus return are behavior, so they belong in a keyboard spec. The strongest distractor is option 1: subtree scoping really is a known axe failure mode, which makes 'the scan could not see the dialog' sound expert, but the premise is that the scan ran and stayed green, and widening its scope does not turn a behavioral defect into a rule violation. Option 2 is the conformance overclaim the tooling docs warn against: a clean scan is a regression signal, not a conformance proof, so a keyboard defect is still an accessibility defect. Option 3 overcorrects — the scan is the cheap layer that catches the mechanical subset on every commit, which is exactly why it should stay.

mcqs.question: A repository gates `coverageThreshold: { global: { lines: 87 } }` and sits at 87.2%. A PR adds an untested retry branch to the payment flow, but the ratio rises to 87.4% because other tests landed in the same merge, so the gate is green. Which change makes the gate say something about that PR?
options: Raise the global floor to 95%, so a higher number leaves no room for a payment path to ship untested.
Gate coverage of the changed lines with a floor and review the exclusion list, keeping the aggregate as a regression signal beside behavior assertions.
Exclude the legacy folders from coverage collection, so the percentage describes only the code this team still owns.
Replace the threshold with mutation score on the payment module, so the gate measures assertion strength instead of execution.
mcqs.explanation: Coverage tells you which lines no test executed, never whether the tests that ran asserted anything, so the useful gate is local to the risk: coverage of the changed lines, with exclusions reviewed as part of the diff (https://martinfowler.com/bliki/TestCoverage.html). An aggregate ratio is a budget shared by the whole repository, so thousands of unrelated lines can absorb one untested branch — which is what happened here. The strongest distractor is option 0: raising the floor feels like raising the bar, but the arithmetic is the same, so the next untested payment branch can hide behind the same unrelated tests, and legacy code now blocks merges that never touched it. Option 2 moves the number instead of measuring the change, and an exclusion list nobody reviews is where coverage stops meaning anything; option 3 measures the right property in the wrong place — mutation testing is expensive and belongs on the domain layer as a periodic check, not as the per-PR gate that must answer 'did this diff arrive with tests?'.

mcqs.question: One Playwright spec fails about once in twenty CI runs with 'locator resolved to 0 elements' on `getByRole('status')`, never on a developer machine, and CI runs with `retries: 0` and no trace. What is the right first move?
options: Insert `await page.waitForTimeout(1000)` before the assertion, so the element has time to appear.
Set `retries: 3` in CI so the pipeline stops going red while someone finds time to look at it.
Relax the assertion to `toBeVisible()` on the surrounding container, so a missing status element cannot fail the run.
Reproduce it with repeated runs (`--repeat-each=20`) and capture a trace, then classify the race before changing the test.
mcqs.explanation: A test that changes outcome without a relevant code change is a measurement problem, so the first step is evidence about which kind: reproduce under load or in parallel, then read the trace — DOM snapshots, network, console, action log — to classify a timing race, a state leak, nondeterministic data or a genuine product bug before editing anything (https://playwright.dev/docs/trace-viewer). The strongest distractor is option 1: retries become legitimate once they also capture the failing run (`trace: 'on-first-retry'`), but used alone they turn a 5% race into a green badge and delete the only signal that something is wrong — retry-until-green normalizes flakiness instead of fixing it. Option 0 guesses at the delay and adds a second of runtime to every run without removing the race, and option 2 deletes the assertion that would have caught the missing element, so 'nothing renders' becomes a passing state.

mcqs.question: A mobile client and an API team share an order payload. The API renames `status` to `state`; both repositories' unit suites stay green and the break is found in staging. Which check would have failed in both pipelines before staging?
options: A consumer-driven contract test on the order response: the client publishes the shape it needs and the producer's pipeline verifies it.
A Jest snapshot of a response fixture committed in the client repository, compared on every run.
The existing checkout end-to-end journey, run after merge, which never renders the order status field.
Stricter TypeScript types on the client's `Order` interface, so the compiler rejects the new field.
mcqs.explanation: A contract test encodes an agreement at a boundary, so it lives where disagreement starts: the consumer states the shape it reads and the producer's pipeline checks its own output against that statement, which fails on both sides the moment the rename lands (https://docs.pact.io/). The strongest distractor is option 1: snapshotting a fixture looks like a contract and is the opposite of one — the fixture is a copy the client team wrote, so the comparison asks 'did this copy change?', and it stays green forever while the real producer drifts. Option 2 can only catch what its journey renders, minutes after the merge, and reports it as a UI assertion rather than a named disagreement; option 3 is a compile-time mirror of the same copy, because hand-written types describe what the client believes and nothing checks that belief against the producer.

mcqs.question: Visual baselines were generated on an `ubuntu-22.04` runner. CI moved to `ubuntu-24.04`, the snapshot names still match, and unchanged pages now report about 12k differing pixels. Which fix keeps the pixel contract intact?
options: Raise `maxDiffPixels` until the suite is green again, then tighten it later once the image settles.
Regenerate the baselines on the new image and commit them with the upgrade, so every run starts from a current reference.
Pin the image, fonts, browser build and device scale factor, and generate and compare baselines only in that job.
Replace the screenshots with `toMatchAriaSnapshot`, which is stable across environments and also covers accessibility.
mcqs.explanation: Screenshots differ between browsers and platforms because of rendering, fonts and more, so a baseline is only comparable inside the environment that produced it (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-snapshots); the same platform suffix on a new image is not the same renderer, so the environment itself has to become part of the contract — pinned image, pinned fonts, pinned browser, pinned scale factor — and the comparison runs only there. The strongest distractor is option 1: re-baselining is what teams actually do, and it is how the suite stops protecting anything, because an image bump now ships a commit full of screenshot churn that reviewers approve wholesale, with any genuine 4px layout regression riding along inside it. Option 0 buys the same green with a tolerance that silently accepts small real diffs, and option 3 swaps the contract instead of stabilizing it: an ARIA snapshot covers semantics, not spacing, so the pixel regression it was meant to catch becomes invisible.

mcqs.question: A polling hook calls `setTimeout(poll, 5000)` again from inside `poll`, so the schedule never runs out. A test calls `vi.runAllTimers()` to let one cycle settle. What actually happens?
options: It fires only the callbacks pending at that moment and ignores timers they schedule, so the test settles after a single cycle.

It keeps executing the timers those callbacks re-queue, the queue never empties, and the runner aborts with an 'Aborting after running N timers' error; advance a bounded window with `advanceTimersByTime`, or use `runOnlyPendingTimers` to fire only what is scheduled now.
It falls back to real timers for the re-queued callback, so the second poll runs on wall-clock time and the test becomes slow instead of failing.
It throws immediately, because a timer created inside a timer callback is not registered in the fake clock's queue.
mcqs.explanation: `runAllTimers` drains the queue to exhaustion, which is only meaningful when the queue is finite. A callback that re-arms itself keeps enqueueing, so the runner hits its timer limit and aborts: Jest documents exactly this for recursive timers in its 'Run Pending Timers' section, and prescribes `runOnlyPendingTimers` — fire what is scheduled now, not what it creates (https://jestjs.io/docs/timer-mocks). Vitest exposes the same trio, and its own example shows the bounded pair `advanceTimersByTime` / `advanceTimersToNextTimer` for interval-style code (https://vitest.dev/guide/mocking/timers). The strongest distractor is option 0: it silently swaps the contract of `runAllTimers` for the contract of `runOnlyPendingTimers`, which is the exact confusion that makes a polling test hang or abort in CI while passing when the hook happens to schedule only once. Option 3 inverts the mechanism — re-queued timers are tracked precisely because the callback runs on the fake clock — and option 2 invents a real-clock fallback that fake timers do not have.

mcqs.question: A shared `userBuilder()` in `tests/builders/user.ts` inserts a row into the database and also exposes `assertValid()` helpers. A new test calls `const user = await userBuilder({ active: false })`. What is the design problem?
options: None: writing the row keeps tests isolated, and the assertion inside the builder guarantees the fixture is valid.

Building is no longer pure: construction hides I/O and couples every test that uses it to the database, and the embedded assertion cannot be opted out of; split a pure `build` that returns data from an explicit `create` path for persistence.
Only that `active: false` should be spelled as a named variant such as `suspendedUser()`; accepting inline overrides is what makes scenarios unreadable.
Only that `Partial<User>` lets a test override `id`, and duplicate ids are what make the insert fail.
mcqs.explanation: A builder's value is a valid, boring default plus the handful of overrides the scenario cares about, and that only holds while construction stays pure and predictable; the bank's rule is to keep assertions and I/O out of the builder and put persistence behind an explicit `create` path, so `build` cannot surprise a test with a database round trip. The strongest distractor is option 2: it takes the real principle ('expose named variants for recurring states') and over-generalizes it into 'never accept inline overrides', when overrides are the primary mechanism and named variants only package states that recur often. Option 0 mistakes per-test rows for isolation — isolation is about which data a test owns, not about hiding a write inside a constructor — and option 3 names a genuine typing hazard (loosening `id` in the overrides type) that is a detail, not the design defect.

mcqs.question: A component test runs `render(<UserList />)` and immediately asserts `expect(screen.getByText('No users yet')).toBeInTheDocument()`. It passes locally and fails in CI with 'Unable to find an element'. What is the correct fix, and why?
options: Raise the test timeout: the first render is slower in CI, so the assertion just runs too early.

Use `await screen.findByText('No users yet')`: `findBy` retries the query until the settled empty state appears, while `getBy` asserts the DOM at that instant and throws when the request has not settled.
Use `expect(screen.queryByText('No users yet')).not.toBeInTheDocument()`, because the empty state should not be asserted until the request resolves.
Make the network mock resolve synchronously so the empty state exists on first render and `getByText` becomes valid.
mcqs.explanation: The three query families answer different timing questions: `getBy` says 'it must be there now' and throws otherwise, `queryBy` says 'it may be absent' and returns `null`, and `findBy` waits for eventual appearance by retrying the query until it matches or the timeout expires (https://testing-library.com/docs/dom-testing-library/api-async/). The empty screen is a settled state produced by a request, so it is a `findBy` case by definition. The strongest distractor is option 3: making the mock resolve synchronously does turn the test green, but it deletes the transition the test exists to cover — the component would never render loading, so the loading-to-empty wiring, the very code that was broken, stops being executed. Option 2 is a quieter failure: absence is also true while loading, so the assertion passes even if the empty state never renders at all, which is a permanent no-op dressed as a check. Option 0 addresses a symptom that the retrying query already handles, and elongating timeouts masks exactly this class of race.

mcqs.question: A pull request adds `expect(container).toMatchSnapshot()` for a settings page. The committed baseline is 900 lines of markup and reviewers approve the diff without reading it. Which change actually restores the signal?
options: Run the suite with `--ci` so a new snapshot fails instead of being written, which solves the review problem.

Assert the contract instead — roles, accessible names, values and the state changes that matter — and keep snapshots small and deliberate for stable serialized output; if a structural snapshot stays, normalize volatile fields and review its diff like code.
Split the snapshot into one smaller `toMatchSnapshot()` per child component, keeping the same full-DOM coverage.
Convert it to `toMatchInlineSnapshot()` so the baseline lives next to the assertion and reviewers are forced to read it.
mcqs.explanation: A snapshot is a stored serialization compared against later output, so it only protects something when the serialized form is the contract; a whole rendered tree is mostly incidental markup, which means every wrapper or class change produces a diff nobody can evaluate — the failure mode the bank names as noise (https://jestjs.io/docs/snapshot-testing). Behavior assertions on role, name and value survive refactors that keep the contract intact, and small snapshots over stable structured output keep the deliberate structural check. The strongest distractor is option 2: splitting the same capture into per-component files makes each diff shorter, but the captured object is unchanged, so incidental churn still fails the suite at the same rate — the problem is what is captured, not how it is chopped up. Option 0 is a real guardrail (it stops new baselines being written silently) that does nothing about a 900-line blob being approved unseen, and option 3 relocates the blob into the source file, where review is worse, not better.

scenarios.prompt: A save flow is covered by this Playwright test. It passes locally and fails in CI roughly one run in five with `expect(received).toBe(expected) // false !== true`. Name the defects, rewrite the assertion so it fails only when the behavior is wrong, and explain what you would assert instead if the exact word `Saved` were not the contract.
rubric: Names `isVisible()` as a non-retrying inspection (returns immediately, `timeout` deprecated and ignored) and the boolean assertion as the second half of the same defect.
Rewrites with an awaited web-first assertion on the locator (`toHaveText`/`toBeVisible`) and explains that the retry is the wait, so no sleep or retry is added.
Keeps role-and-name locators and says what they protect (the role and accessible-name contract) instead of falling back to test ids or CSS.
Offers a contract-appropriate alternative when the exact copy is not the contract (stable completion state, URL, or `expect.poll` for non-DOM observables).
Describes verification — repeated runs or a trace on failure — rather than accepting a single green run.

scenarios.prompt: `Editor` is covered only by the test below. Since it was written, the client started unwrapping a `{ data }` envelope and mapping server error codes to banner messages, and the component renders `savedAt` plus a per-code error. The test still passes. Explain what the mock hides, replace it with a boundary mock, name the cases you would keep, and say how you would prove the new test can fail.
rubric: Names what the function spy deletes (request building, envelope unwrap, error mapping) and that it freezes an old payload shape.
Moves the mock to the HTTP boundary with a request-handler setup and resets handlers between tests.
Covers success and a mapped failure through the real client, asserting visible outcomes (status, alert, draft preserved) instead of the mock.
Assigns the remaining layers explicitly: contract test for the envelope, one e2e journey, and a narrow unit test where a function mock is legitimate.
Explains how to prove the test can fail (mutate the parser or the error branch) and keeps isolation (`onUnhandledRequest`, `resetHandlers`).

scenarios.prompt: A confirmation dialog is covered by the code below. The last redesign changed spacing — which is fine — and removed the dialog's accessible name, which is a regression. Say which layer should fail for each kind of change, then design the assertions and the CI review so the next change of either kind fails for the right reason.
rubric: Explains that the current test asserts nothing semantic and can screenshot or scan an unsettled state.
Adds the dialog's role-and-accessible-name assertion as the layer that owns the name regression, after waiting for the settled dialog.
Adds a keyboard/focus spec (Escape, focus return, containment) as behavior no automated scan evaluates.
Keeps the screenshot deterministic (animations disabled, masked volatile regions, pinned image) and describes a review policy for baseline diffs.
Places the scan correctly: scoped to the dialog, a rule-based safety net that neither proves conformance nor judges whether a name is meaningful.

scenarios.prompt: This test is meant to prove that `SearchBox` debounces its `onSearch` callback. In CI it times out; once a teammate adds `delay: null` to silence that, it goes green without proving anything about debouncing. Identify each defect, then rewrite it with fake timers so the test fails if the debounce is removed, fails if the delay is ignored, and still never sleeps or retries.
rubric: Connects the interaction to the fake clock (`userEvent.setup({ advanceTimers: vi.advanceTimersByTime })`, or an equivalent explicit driving of the clock) and explains that the timeout comes from user-event's faked internal delay.
Asserts both edges — nothing at `DEBOUNCE_MS - 1`, exactly one call after crossing the delay — so the test fails when the debounce is removed, instead of only checking an eventual call.
Covers the reset case (a keystroke inside the window restarts it, producing a single trailing call with the final value) and asserts the call argument, not just the call count.
Keeps the clock lifecycle in `beforeEach` / `afterEach` and restores real timers, flushing pending timers before restoring rather than leaking the fake clock into later tests.
Rejects sleeps, arbitrary `waitFor` timeouts, and `runAllTimers` on self-rescheduling work; awaits the observable result when the debounced callback is asynchronous.
